introduction-what-are-metrics.core: A metric is a number measured over time: request count, latency, memory used. Each sample is cheap (a timestamp and a float), so metrics can be kept for months, aggregated across thousands of instances, and alerted on in real time. They answer 'is something wrong and how much?' but not 'why exactly?'. That's what logs and traces add.

first_principles.problem: A team only has logs and must grep millions of lines to learn whether error rates went up.

analogy.title: A car dashboard
analogy.story: Speed, fuel and temperature tell you at a glance whether things are fine, but not why the engine light is on.
analogy.breaks: Dashboards show one car; metrics aggregate fleets.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Error rate computable across all pods in one query.

code.text:
# HELP http_requests_total Total HTTP requests
# TYPE http_requests_total counter
http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/api/orders",status="200"} 18342
http_requests_total{method="GET",route="/api/orders",status="500"} 27

check.q: What question do metrics answer well, and which do they answer poorly?
check.a: They're great for 'is something wrong and how much'; poor at 'why did this specific request fail'.

the-four-core-metric-types.core: Counters only go up (requests, errors, bytes) and reset on restart; you use their rate. Gauges go up and down (memory, queue depth, temperature) and you read their current value. Histograms count observations into buckets (latency ≤100 ms, ≤250 ms...) so you can compute quantiles across instances. Summaries compute quantiles client-side, which is accurate per instance but impossible to aggregate across them.

first_principles.problem: A team records latency as a gauge of the last request's duration and misses all the slow requests between scrapes.

analogy.title: Odometer, fuel gauge, and a speed-band tally
analogy.story: The odometer only increases, the fuel gauge rises and falls, and a tally of 'how many minutes in each speed band' describes the whole trip.
analogy.breaks: Odometers don't reset on restart; counters do, and rate() handles it.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Rate, saturation and latency distribution all captured.

code.text:
from prometheus_client import Counter, Gauge, Histogram
REQS = Counter("http_requests_total", "Requests", ["route", "status"])
INFLIGHT = Gauge("http_inflight_requests", "In-flight")
LAT = Histogram("http_request_duration_seconds", "Latency", ["route"],
                buckets=[.025, .05, .1, .25, .5, 1, 2.5])

@INFLIGHT.track_inprogress()
def handle(route):
    with LAT.labels(route).time():
        ...
    REQS.labels(route, "200").inc()

check.q: Why are histograms preferred over summaries in Prometheus?
check.a: Histogram buckets can be summed across instances to compute fleet-wide quantiles; summary quantiles can't be aggregated.

metric-types-measuring-distributions-his.core: Averages hide pain: a 50 ms mean can hide 2% of requests taking 5 s. Distributions need percentiles (p50, p95, p99). Histograms store cumulative bucket counts, and histogram_quantile() interpolates within the bucket where the quantile falls, so accuracy depends on bucket boundaries placed around your SLO thresholds. Native or exponential histograms adapt bucket resolution automatically.

first_principles.problem: Average latency looks healthy at 80 ms while 1 in 50 users waits 4 seconds.

analogy.title: Exam results by grade band
analogy.story: Knowing 'average score 70' is less useful than how many students failed; bands show the spread.
analogy.breaks: Grade bands are fixed; histogram buckets must be chosen thoughtfully.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows tail latency per route across all pods.

code.text:
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
# fraction under 300 ms SLO threshold:
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.25"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

check.q: Why can't you average p99 values from several instances?
check.a: Percentiles aren't additive; you must aggregate the underlying bucket counts and then compute the quantile.

the-power-of-labels.core: Labels (key=value pairs) turn one metric into many series: http_requests_total{service, route, status, region}. They let you slice and aggregate: errors by route, latency by region, saturation by pod. Each unique label combination is a separate stored time series, so labels must have bounded values. Use route templates (/users/:id), not raw URLs, and status classes, not user IDs.

first_principles.problem: A team can't tell which endpoint is failing because all requests are counted in one unlabelled metric.
derivation: Add labels for **dimensions you query by**.

analogy.title: Tags on library books
analogy.story: Tagging by genre and language lets you find all French mysteries; tagging by reader's name would create a tag per person.
analogy.breaks: Extra tags cost libraries little; each label value costs memory in a TSDB.

code.text:
sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
# top 3 failing routes
topk(3, sum by (route) (rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])))

check.q: Why use route templates like /users/:id instead of raw paths as label values?
check.a: Raw paths contain unbounded IDs, creating a new time series per user and exploding cardinality.

the-danger-of-high-cardinality.core: Cardinality is the number of unique series: the product of distinct label values. Ten routes × five statuses × 100 pods is 5,000 series. Add user_id with a million values and you get 5 billion. Each series costs memory in the TSDB head block and index, so high cardinality causes out-of-memory crashes, slow queries and huge bills. Watch series counts and enforce limits.

first_principles.problem: Adding a customer_id label to one metric crashes the Prometheus server overnight.

analogy.title: A filing cabinet with a drawer per combination
analogy.story: Adding 'customer' as a sorting dimension turns 50 drawers into 50 million.
analogy.breaks: Cabinets fill slowly; cardinality spikes in one deploy.

code.text:
topk(10, count by (__name__) ({__name__=~".+"}))
# series per label value for a metric
count by (customer_id) (api_calls_total)

collecting-metrics-push-vs-pull.core: Pull (Prometheus): targets expose /metrics and the server scrapes them on an interval using service discovery. You get built-in up/down detection, control over load, and easy local debugging. Push (StatsD, OTLP, Pushgateway): apps send metrics to a collector, which suits short-lived jobs, serverless and clients behind NAT. Modern stacks mix both, often via the OpenTelemetry Collector.

first_principles.problem: A nightly batch job finishes before Prometheus scrapes it, so its metrics never appear.

analogy.title: A meter reader vs mailing in readings
analogy.story: The utility visits each house to read the meter (pull), but holiday cabins mail their reading in (push).
analogy.breaks: Mailed readings can be late; pushed metrics lack scrape-based health signals.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Alert if last success older than 26 h.

code.text:
from prometheus_client import CollectorRegistry, Gauge, push_to_gateway
reg = CollectorRegistry()
last = Gauge("job_last_success_unixtime", "Last success", registry=reg)
last.set_to_current_time()
push_to_gateway("pushgateway:9091", job="nightly_export", registry=reg)

check.q: What useful signal do you get for free with pull-based collection?
check.a: The up metric, telling you when a target can't be scraped (down or unreachable).

exporters-the-universal-adapters.core: Many systems (Linux hosts, MySQL, Redis, Nginx, cloud APIs, hardware) don't speak Prometheus natively. Exporters are small processes that query them (procfs, stats endpoints, SQL, SNMP) and expose /metrics. node_exporter, blackbox_exporter (probes HTTP, TCP, ICMP and DNS from outside), mysqld_exporter, cloudwatch_exporter and the OTel Collector receivers are the standard toolkit.

first_principles.problem: The team needs database, host and external endpoint metrics, but none of those systems expose Prometheus format.
truths: Systems expose stats in their own formats.

analogy.title: Interpreters at an international meeting
analogy.story: Each delegate speaks their own language; interpreters translate into the common language everyone records.
analogy.breaks: Interpreters understand nuance; exporters only expose what they implement.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: probe_success and probe_duration_seconds for the site.

check.q: What does blackbox_exporter measure that node_exporter doesn't?
check.a: Externally observed availability and latency of endpoints (HTTP, TCP, DNS, ICMP), the user's view.
